caption:
Mr Turtle sat bolt upright all day and ended up more tired, not less. Research suggests there's no strong link between how people sit or stand and whether they get back or neck pain. Plenty of people with 'bad' posture have none, and the reverse is true too.

What usually bothers us is staying in one position for hours, even a textbook one. Slouching on the couch is fine. If it starts to ache, take that as a nudge to move.

Hybi's habit: a gentle reminder every 30 minutes to shift, stand or stretch, mixing sitting, standing and walking through the day, plus regular walks and a couple of strength sessions a week. Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios can help. Book online via the link in bio 🐢

caption:
Mr Turtle bought a standing desk and his back still grumbles. Standing desks are genuinely handy because they make it easy to change position. On their own, though, they're not a solution for back or neck pain.

Stand still all day and the feet, legs and lower back start to ache instead. That's one static posture swapped for another. The goal is variety: sit, stand, walk and move.

Hybi's setup: desk at about elbow height, screen at eye level, a soft mat or supportive shoes. Switch every 30 to 45 minutes, stand for calls, sit for focused work, and take a short walk every hour. Regular activity outside work tends to matter more than any piece of furniture. Book online via the link in bio 🐢

caption:
Lulu tiles floors and works low to the ground all day. Every time she stands up, the front of her knee throbs.

At the front of the knee sit a small fluid-filled sac called a bursa and the patellar tendon. Hours of kneeling can leave them irritated.

Hybi's knee saver: wear thick knee pads that stay put and replace them once the foam flattens. Alternate kneeling, squatting and a low stool every 10 to 15 minutes. Sit-to-stands a few times a week help the thighs too.

A hot, red or very swollen knee, locking, giving way, or pain after a knock that persists is worth an assessment. Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can help, including with NSW WorkCover claims. Book online via the link in bio 🦘

caption:
Lulu's back went while lifting a pack of tiles. She couldn't stand up straight and feared the worst.

Most back pain, even the kind that stops you standing tall, is not damage, and it usually settles within a few weeks. Three signs it's the common kind: a clear moment it started, it changes with position, and it stays in the back or buttock without leg tingling or weakness. That pattern responds to movement and time.

A few things do need a prompt check: groin numbness, bladder or bowel changes, worsening leg weakness, fever, or pain after a serious fall.

sections.heading: 1. Five slow rib breaths

caption:
Every time the bridge gets hard, Momo holds her breath. Afterwards her neck feels it more than her tummy.

Most people hold their breath when a movement gets tough. It often adds tension through the neck and jaw and makes control harder. A simple starting point: breathe in to prepare, breathe out through the hardest part. A slow out-breath helps you feel the deep tummy and pelvic floor muscles switch on.

Hybi's 1-minute rib breathing: lie down, knees bent, hands on your lower ribs. In through the nose for four, out through the mouth for six. Five rounds before bed.

caption:
Momo loves a stretch, but Pilates is new to her. Mat class or reformer class? The more she googles, the more confusing it gets.

Mat Pilates uses your bodyweight and small props. It's easy to keep going at home or while travelling, and gets surprisingly hard once you slow down. The reformer's springs can assist or add resistance, so exercises scale in small steps. That often suits people returning from injury or new to exercise.

Neither wins overall. Plenty of people do guided reformer sessions plus a short mat routine at home in between.

slides.heading: Get it checked if you notice

caption:
Momo is always the bendiest in class. Deep stretches feel great, then her joints ache.

Some people's joints move further than average. That isn't a problem on its own, but muscles may have to work harder to control that range, which can lead to aches. Bendy isn't the same as strong.

Hybi's control practice: park the deep end-range stretches and work in the middle of your range. Go slow, use lighter springs and smaller movements, and notice which muscles are working. Add load bit by bit. Research suggests strength training helps many very flexible people.

Joints that often partly slip, widespread aches or unusual tiredness are worth an assessment. The Pilates team at Hybrid Physio builds programs around control. Book online via the link in bio 🐱
